target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would reduce scheduling barriers and increase voting access for many people
objection: A federal Election Day holiday would not reliably remove voting barriers for low-income workers, because federal law does not require private employers to give paid time off for federal holidays. Many low-income workers in retail and service jobs would still have to work or would face unpaid time off, so the policy could fail to solve—and could even worsen—their opportunity-cost barriers.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday is a reliable way to increase turnout
objection: If a voting-access reform does not reliably give working people paid or protected time to vote, it is unlikely to substantially increase turnout. By that standard, a holiday is less reliable than state laws requiring employer time off for voting.

target: AG1’s broader claim that an Election Day holiday would meaningfully boost turnout on its own
objection: Research indicates that election-day holidays by themselves are not an effective way to increase voter turnout compared with other voting-access reforms, so a holiday would not be expected to produce meaningful turnout gains on its own.

target: AG2’s claim that low-income workers would mainly be harmed because a holiday does not guarantee paid time off
objection: Low-income workers’ barriers are not just lost wages or unpaid time; they also include childcare and transportation disruptions. A holiday can reduce those disruptions by changing daytime school and work schedules, making voting more feasible even if some workers still face wage-related costs.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would reduce barriers for low-income voters by changing schedules
objection: Many polling places are in schools and other community facilities that reduce operations on holidays, and transportation and voter-assistance services also often run with reduced hours or staffing. So a national holiday would make polling places and voter assistance less available, not more.

target: AG2’s argument that a holiday must guarantee paid/protected time to affect turnout
objection: Turnout is not determined only by whether workers get guaranteed paid or protected time. Making voting feel like a civic celebration can increase the perceived importance of participation and motivate people to vote even if some practical costs remain.

target: AG2’s claim that low-income workers would still be hurt because federal holidays do not require private employers to provide paid leave
objection: Even without a legal requirement, many private employers and public institutions close or reduce/adjust shifts on federal holidays. That means a national Election Day holiday can still reduce opportunity-cost barriers for many low-income workers rather than simply shifting costs onto them.

target: AG2’s claim that a national holiday is not a viable scheduling reform
objection: Weekend or holiday election scheduling is a broadly viable policy approach, as shown by the fact that many OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays. That suggests a national holiday is a legitimate way to address scheduling constraints on voting.

target: AG1’s claim that low-income workers would gain enough time from a holiday to vote
objection: A federal holiday does not reliably ensure that low-income workers get paid or protected time to vote, because many of them work in retail, service, or essential jobs where holiday schedules continue or workers must still request time off. So the policy may not meaningfully improve access for the workers who face the biggest barriers.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday would help low-income workers more than it hurts them
objection: If low-income workers still have to absorb lost wages or unpaid time, then making Election Day a federal holiday can disadvantage them by increasing or failing to reduce the cost of voting.

target: AG1’s comparison of a holiday with enforceable state time-off laws and automatic voter registration
objection: State laws requiring employer time off for voting can impose enforceable obligations rather than relying on private scheduling decisions, and automatic voter registration reduces administrative barriers without depending on employer behavior. Those reforms are more reliable than a federal holiday.

target: AG1’s argument that many workers would simply get time off on a federal holiday
objection: Voting in person also takes time to travel, wait in line, and complete the ballot. Even if work or school is closed, low-income voters still face those time costs, and holiday scheduling can increase polling-place congestion and wait times by bringing more people out at the same time.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would not reduce opportunity costs for low-income workers
objection: Low-income workers are often constrained mainly by daytime work and school schedules. A national holiday would reduce the need to miss shifts or take unpaid leave, and because holiday scheduling often eases work and school conflicts, it would lower the overall opportunity cost of voting for those workers.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday reliably reduces opportunity costs for low-income voters
objection: The time required to travel, wait, and vote is itself an opportunity cost for low-income voters, even when it does not overlap with work or school. Since a holiday does not eliminate that time burden, it would not reliably reduce opportunity costs for the group facing the biggest barriers.

target: AG2’s claim that in-person voting costs remain the same regardless of holiday status
objection: For low-income voters, the main burden comes from in-person voting conflicting with work and school hours. A national holiday reduces those conflicts, and it can also make childcare and transportation easier to coordinate, so the net opportunity cost would be lower even though travel and waiting still take time.

target: AG1’s assumption that a holiday would not worsen polling access
objection: Holiday scheduling can increase same-day in-person demand enough to raise wait times, while polling-place capacity and staffing may also be reduced if election workers or host facilities are less available on a federal holiday. That means a holiday can systematically make polling access less reliable and increase delays.
